THE CHINA PRESS, SUNDAY, MAY 29, 1921

FORMER SHANGHAI
MAN AND HIS WIFE
ATTACKED BY MOB

Mr. And Mrs. J. E. Tobinson
Set Upon In
Potsdam

Many Shanghai people will read with interest of an incident which befell a former local resident—Mr. J. E. Tobinson, previously with Thomas W. Simmons & Co. here—and his bride while they were passing through Berlin. While watching the funeral procession of the late Kaiserin in Potsdam, Mr. and Mrs. Tobinson were set upon by a mob which pelted them with stones and umbrellas on the accusation that they were "French people" who had made remarks derogatory to the late Empress.

Mr. Tobinson, who left China some months ago, was until about 1 year ago an engineer in the Thomas W. Simmons & Co. offices here and was well known to many Shanghai residents. He and Mrs. Tobinson were married about five months ago and were traveling to the United States by way of Europe.

Mr. Tobinson was born in Russia and went to America with an elder brother some 25 years ago, locating in Chicago. The brother took up law, attaining prominence in the profession, while Mr. Tobinson studied engineering. After the last revolution in Russia the brother returned to that country, joining the Bolshevik faction and became prominent in its activities. A short time ago he rose to one of the leading positions in the Far Eastern government.

The following account of the attack on the Tobinsons in Potsdam is an Associated Press despatch to the New York Times, dated at Berlin April 20:

James E. Tobinson and his wife, residents of Chicago, were attacked by a crowd of German men, women and children Tuesday as they sat on the terrace of Sans Souci Park, following the funeral of former Empress Augusta Victoria.

The Americans were rescued by a security policeman and two German civilians, who locked arms and surrounded them, accepting a pelting of sticks, stones and umbrellas in defense of the couple until they were able to escort them to the police station in Potsdam. Here a patrol of extra policemen was summoned and dispersed the crowd.

During the attack the policemen and the two German civilians were unable to quiet the crowd, members of which were shouting, "Foreigners," "French people." Nor could they entirely shield the Americans.

Mr. Tobinson was beaten about the head and shoulders and his face received a bruised nose. Also his hat was torn from her head, her hair was pulled and she was struck on her arms and body by umbrellas.

Potsdam Police Headquarters in its report concerning the case said: "The Americans were not to blame and they desire that there be no further mention of the affair."

"The mob," said Mr. Tobinson, "was incited by an old woman who thought we were French. The crowd attacked us and chased us from Sans Souci Park to Potsdam. It is my opinion that we would have been killed except for one policeman and two German civilians. The police, however, did all that was possible. I cannot complain of their conduct and desire to make no representations to the German Government."

Mrs. Tobinson, who is a graduate of a college in Valparaiso, Ind., which her husband, a civil engineer, also attended, said:

"We were sitting on the terrace in Sans Souci Park speaking English. There were three women sitting in the same seat. The one nearest us turned to her companions and declared we were French. They began abusing foreigners. I could not understand what they said; but I realised that the women were very angry.

"A crowd gathered. Among it was a number of children. The children, the old woman and others we had spoken in French words derogatory to the former Empress. Neither of us understands French. One of the old woman's companions tried to explain that we had not spoken at all about the dead former Empress but that we were discussing the beauty of the park and regretting that we had no films for our camera.

"The crowd, however, drew nearer, shouting that we were French, and the children began to throw stones. I was so frightened I thought I was choking. The crowd struck my husband with canes and umbrellas. He tried to protect me as we ran, and then two civilians and the policeman came to our aid. There were several hundred persons following us before we reached the police station."

Mr. Tobinson, who said he resided at 2748 West Washburn Avenue, Chicago, when questioned at the police station, declared he and his wife were born in Russia.

Mrs. Tobinson, he asserted, is the daughter of American parents, but that he is a naturalised citizen. He said he could speak neither Russian nor French. He has been in China for Thomas W. Simmons & Co., but now is in business for himself.

Mr. and Mrs. Tobinson have been married for five months. They have visited China, Japan and Italy, and Mr. Tobinson also has made a trip to Siberia.

《字林西报》，1921年5月29日，星期日

前上海居民及其妻子
遭暴民袭击

J. E. Tobinson 夫妇
在波茨坦
遭到围攻

许多上海人会有兴趣读到一则发生在前本地居民——此前在本市托马斯·W·西蒙斯公司（Thomas W. Simmons & Co.）任职的 J. E. Tobinson 先生——及其新娘途经柏林时遭遇的事件。当在波茨坦观看已故皇后葬礼游行队伍时，Tobinson 夫妇遭到一群暴民袭击，暴民向他们投掷石块和雨伞，指控他们是发表了对已故皇后不敬言论的“法国人”。

Tobinson 先生数月前离开中国，直到约一年前一直是本市托马斯·W·西蒙斯公司办事处的工程师，为许多上海居民所熟知。他与 Tobinson 太太于约五个月前结婚，正经由欧洲前往美国。

Tobinson 先生出生于俄国，约25年前与兄长一同前往美国，定居芝加哥。其兄从事法律职业，在该行业崭露头角，而 Tobinson 先生则研习工程学。在俄国最近一次革命后，其兄返回该国，加入布尔什维克派系，并在其活动中变得显赫。不久前，他升任远东政府的主要职位之一。

以下是美联社发给《纽约时报》关于 Tobinson 夫妇在波茨坦遇袭的报道，发自柏林，4月20日：

芝加哥居民 James E. Tobinson 及其妻子周二在前皇后奥古斯塔·维多利亚葬礼结束后，坐在无忧宫公园（Sans Souci Park）的露台上时，遭到一群德国男女老少的袭击。

美国人被一名治安警察和两名德国平民救出，这些人挽起手臂围住他们，替这对夫妇承受棍棒、石块和雨伞的投击，直到能够护送他们前往波茨坦警察局。此处增派了一队警察驱散了人群。

在袭击过程中，警察和两名德国平民无法使人群平静下来，人群中有人高喊“外国人”、“法国人”。他们也未能完全保护美国人。

Tobinson 先生头部和肩部遭殴打，面部鼻子淤青。此外，他的帽子从她头上被扯掉，她的头发被拉扯，手臂和身体被雨伞击打。

波茨坦警察总局在有关此案的报告中称：“美国人没有过错，他们希望不再提及此事。”

“暴民，”Tobinson 先生说，“是由一位以为我们是法国人的老妇人煽动的。人群攻击我们，并将我们从无忧宫公园追赶到波茨坦。我认为，若非有一名警察和两名德国平民相助，我们恐怕已被杀害。然而，警方已尽力而为。我对他们的行为无可抱怨，也不愿向德国政府提出任何交涉。”

Tobinson 太太毕业于印第安纳州瓦尔帕莱索（Valparaiso, Ind.）的一所学院，她的丈夫、土木工程师也曾就读于此，她说：

“我们坐在无忧宫公园的露台上用英语交谈。同一张座位上坐着三位女士。离我们要近的一位转向同伴，声称我们是法国人。她们开始辱骂外国人。我听不懂她们说什么；但我意识到这些妇女非常愤怒。

“人群聚集起来。其中包括一些儿童。孩子们、老妇人和其他人说我们用法语说了对已故皇后不敬的话。我们俩都不懂法语。老妇人的一位同伴试图解释，说我们根本没有谈论已故皇后，而是在讨论公园的美景，并遗憾我们的相机没有胶卷。

“然而，人群越靠越近，高喊我们是法国人，孩子们开始扔石头。我吓得以为自己窒息了。人群用手杖和雨伞殴打我丈夫。我们在逃跑时他试图保护我，随后两名平民和一名警察前来援助。在我们到达警察局之前，有数百人跟随我们。”

Tobinson 先生在警察局接受询问时称，他居住在芝加哥西沃什伯恩大道（West Washburn Avenue）2748号，并声明他和妻子均出生于俄国。

他断言，Tobinson 太太是美国父母的女儿，而他本人是归化公民。他说他既不会说俄语也不会说法语。他曾在中国为托马斯·W·西蒙斯公司工作，但现在自己经商。

Tobinson 夫妇结婚已五个月。他们访问过中国、日本和意大利，Tobinson 先生还曾去过西伯利亚。

REPORT ON Mr. Hodoroff.

Made by D. S. I. Sullivan Forwarded by Chief Detective Officer.

Sir,
Mr. Hodoroff, who is said to be a lawyer by profession,
first came to Shanghai on the S. S. "Penza" on April 9th 1919,
along with Semeshko, Klassing and Col. Tolstoff.
He and Col. Tolstoff stayed at 25A North Szechuen Road,
where they were frequently visited by Agarioff, a former Mayor
of Vladivostock.
There was information that Hodoroff and Semeshko when
they first came to Shanghai brought with them several millions
of Russian money but confirmation of the report could not be
obtained.
After some time Hodoroff went to Tientsin where he is
said to have been either employed by Zimmerman & Co., or to
have stayed with an employee of that firm.
He returned to Shanghai on the 4th instant and stayed
with Mr. Haas at 19 Quinsan Gardens until the 11th instant
when he left Shanghai by the 7.55 a.m. train for Tientsin.
He did not receive any visitors at Mr. Haas' house, but
he was out most of the time.
Hodoroff is said to have been appointed Procurator
(a post equivalent to that of Crown Advocate in the British
Court) to the Court at Vladivostock, but owing to recent
events in that port he has delayed going there.

I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
J. Sullivan.
D. S. I.

关于 Hodoroff 先生的报告。

由副督察长 Sullivan 撰写，经首席侦探官转发。

阁下，
据称职业为律师的 Hodoroff 先生，于1919年4月9日随 Semeshko、Klassing 和 Tolstoff 上校乘“奔萨”号轮船首次抵达上海。
他与 Tolstoff 上校住在北四川路25A号，前符拉迪沃斯托克市长 Agarioff 经常拜访此地。
有消息称 Hodoroff 和 Semeshko 初到上海时带来了数百万卢布，但未能证实该报告。
一段时间后，Hodoroff 前往天津，据说受雇于 Zimmerman & Co.，或与该公司的一名雇员同住。
他于本月4日返回上海，住在昆山路花园（Quinsan Gardens）19号的 Haas 先生处，直至本月11日乘上午7:55的火车离开上海前往天津。
他在 Haas 先生家中未接待任何访客，但大部分时间外出。
据称 Hodoroff 曾被任命为符拉迪沃斯托克法院的检察官（相当于英国法院的王室辩护律师一职），但由于该港口最近发生的事件，他推迟了前往那里。

此致，
敬礼
J. Sullivan.

( 2nd February 1920.

Dear Captain Barrett,

I personally consider the present moment most inopportune
for holding political meetings in the Foreign Settlement which
is hardly a suitable arena for politicians without distinction of
parties. As Mr. Agareff and others have applied to the Police
for permission, I would suggest that the Police declines to
issue the permit without stating any special reason.

If you, however, deem it necessary, could you perhaps advice the
petitioners to apply to me as their application has no doubt a
political aspect. I will in that case refer the matter to my
Minister who I believe will share my views.

Yours sincerely

V. Grosse(signed)

Captain E.I.M. Barrett,             Consul General for Russia.
Acting Commissioner of Police.

亲爱的 Barrett 上尉，

我个人认为，目前是在外国租界举行政治会议的最不合时宜的时刻，这里并非不分党派的政治家们的合适舞台。鉴于 Agareff 先生等人已向警方申请许可，我建议警方在不说明任何特殊理由的情况下拒绝发放许可证。

根据内务省的指示，横滨警察局长昨天上午传唤俄国臣民 James E. Tobinson 到其办公室，并以在日本传播布尔什维克宣传为由命令将其驱逐出境。Tobinson 和他的妻子去年9月从美国来到该国，住在横滨山下町66号的 Maisonette 酒店。今年年初，他们去西伯利亚旅行了数月。Tobinson 被指控从布尔什维克总部收取了一大笔钱，据说警方掌握着包括证实其行为的信件和文件在内的充分证据。Tobinson 还被指控在去年秋天来到该国之前，曾在芝加哥从事传播布尔什维克宣传活动数年。他和他的妻子于昨天下午乘船前往上海。

Chapei Police Are Over Curious
After he had stepped on the platform from a train at the North Station last night at nine o'clock, the Inspector of Police from Erkutsk was accosted by Chapei police and asked for his passport and other identification. According to the story the police did not understand him and without proceeding to make proper inquiry, treated him roughly.
Accompanied by his family, the Inspector of Police, proceeded to various hotels in an effort to find lodging followed by the police. He lodged a complaint with the Russian Consulate this morning against the action of the Chapei police.
Concerning the large sum of money that Semeshko and Hodoroff are said to have brought to Shanghai there is no way at present of confirming the rumour. Semeshko is living in very poor lodgings and as far as can be ascertained lives very frugally and there is nothing to show that he possesses much wealth. REPORT ON Rumours of Bolshevik meeting.

Made by D. I. Cruickshank Forwarded by

Sir,

I beg most respectfully to report, that, I have made enquiry re the alleged movement of Bolsheviks, but cannot find the least signs to justify such rumours. Unquestionably there are Bolsheviks in Shanghai, but I cannot find any person, who has known any one to declare himself such, unless sailors from the Russian merchants ships, who I am informed, many declare openly to believe in Bolshevism.

Amongst passengers arriving from America, there are always a certain per cent of them of Russian extract, but whatever their sympathies are. They would not be likely to declare openly. I believe there may be an attempt to spread Bolshevik propaganda, but most likely such will come from Chinese Agents. I am informed there are many such persons in Harbour and vicinity.

I may also point out, that, the Revolutionist Chinese have little to learn regarding Bolshevism. For we have been subjected to nothing else for many years, but Bolshevism in the way of armed robberies and bomb outrages.

I am, Sir,

Your obedient servant,
James Cruickshank
Detective Inspector.

先生，

我谨恭敬地报告，我已就所谓的布尔什维克活动进行了调查，但找不到任何迹象证明此类谣言属实。毫无疑问，上海有布尔什维克，但我找不到任何认识自称是布尔什维克的人，除非是来自俄国商船的水手，据我所知，许多水手公开宣称信仰布尔什维克主义。

我还要指出，革命派的中国人关于布尔什维克主义没什么可学的。因为多年来我们遭受的无非就是武装抢劫和炸弹袭击形式的布尔什维克主义。

REPORT ON Bolshevist Activities in Shanghai and Licensing of
Boarding-Houses.
Made by W. Givens Forwarded by Chief Detective Officer.
Sir,
There seems to be some ground for the reports that the
Bolsheviks intend to make Shanghai a centre for their propaganda.
To check their activities, the police will need to be informed
on the movements and doings of Russians, whose antecedents are
unknown, and their friends. It is very hard to obtain this
information in the absence of any regulations governing boarding-
houses. As a temporary measure, I beg to suggest that the
Russian Consul be requested to empower the Police to visit all
Russian boarding houses, as often as they think fit, for the
purpose of interrogating and obtaining full information about
their guests.
As the suppression of Bolshevicism is something in which all
nations are interested, and as it is necessary to have boarding
houses in Shanghai under police control so that the S. M. P.
can effectively assist in this work, I respectfully take the
liberty of again directing your attention to the necessity of
licensing these establishments.
The attached is a list of Russian boarding houses, information
about whose guests would appear desirable from a police point of
view. The list, which has been hurriedly compiled, does not
purport to be complete.
I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
W. Givens

先生，
有理由相信布尔什维克意图将上海作为其宣传中心的报告并非空穴来风。为了遏制他们的活动，警方需要掌握背景不明的俄国人及其朋友的动向和行为。由于缺乏管理寄宿公寓的法规，很难获得这些信息。作为一项临时措施，我建议请求俄国领事授权警方随时访问所有俄国寄宿公寓，以便审问住客并获取关于他们的完整信息。
鉴于镇压布尔什维克主义是所有国家都感兴趣的事，且有必要将上海的寄宿公寓置于警方控制之下，以便上海公共租界工部局警务处 (S. M. P.) 能有效协助此项工作，我冒昧再次提请阁下注意对这些场所颁发执照的必要性。

to the Russian Volunteer Fleet are in the habit of bringing
letters from Bolsheviks in Vladivostock to Russians in

sailors' quarters on these boats may unearth correspondence
which would throw some light on Bolshevist activities in
Shanghai. A poem in pamphlet form, a translation of an extract

From Vladivostok
To H.M. Consul General, Shanghai.
Despatched March 19, 1919. Received Shanghai March 20.

Following for Major Hilton-Johnson from General
Blair,-
1. Information has been received from Russian sources
to the effect that a Bolsheviks conference is to be
held in Shanghai about the end of March. Four delegates
from Omsk are reported to be now on their way to
Shanghai, while four delegates from the Maritime
Provinces and possibly other Russian delegates are
to meet Japanese and local Shanghai delegates. There
will also ppobably be several from the United States.
Further information is expected.

2. The Bolsheviks are reported to be sending
agitators with large sums of money to China and
the Far East.

3. With reference to Para. 1, it is reliably reported
from an American source that the conference at Shanghai
is fixed for the 22nd March, that delegates from Soviet
Russia are already there, that 20 are going from Siberia,
of whom four are from Vladivostok, and that the business
is, firstly, the organisation of an armed rising in
Siberia, secondly, Bolshevik propaganda in China, Japan,
and the United States, and lastly, the formation of a
direct liaison with the Bolsheviks in Germany and Poland.
